VENGEANCE.
Terrible Condition of Affairs in Indian Territory-A Bloody Battle Imminent.
VINITA, I. T., August 3.—On the 26th of July two Creek negro cattle thieves, named Manlay and Jones, were hanged near Gibson Station, Creek Nation, it is supposed by Texas cattle men, who had lost sixteen cattle while driving through that neighborhood. This seems to have aroused the colored men of the Creek Nation, who accused the Cherokees of hanging the thieves. On Tuesday morning thirteen negroes crossed into the Cherokee side, swearing they would kill the first Cherokee they met. Two Cherokee boys named Cobb and Cowan, who had been to Gilson, returning home were met by these black devils and fired upon. Cowan was badly wounded in the face, and his horse became frightened and ran away, carrying him out of their reach.

Young Cobb showed fight, and leaping off his horse began returning the fire, falling back as fast as he emptied his revolver, loading as he ran toward his uncle's house, a mile away, but was shot down when near the house, and died in three hours.

The Cherokees are greatly incensed, and have demanded the thirteen negroes of the Creek Chief, giving him until tonight to surrender them, when, if they are not given up, they declare they will go after them.

The Creeks are said to be willing to surrender the negroes, but it is thought they will not be able to do so, the negroes being too strong for them.

It was difficult for Chiefs Bushyhead and Adair to restrain the Cherokees from immediate vengeance, and they will be unable to keep them off the Creek territory longer than to-morrow morning.

bill-peters-muscogee-1880-07-09.A2:
CREEKS VS. CHIEROKEES.
VINITA, I. T., Aug. 4.—On the 26th ult. two negro Creekes were hanged. The Creekes accused the Cherokees, and vowed to kill the first of them they met. On Tuesday thirteen negroes crossed on the Cherokee side for vengeance. Cobb and Cowan, two Cherokee boys, were encountered. Cowan was badly wounded, and Cobb, after a determined fight, was killed.

The Cherokees are greatly incensed, and have demanded the thirteen negroes of the Creek Chief, giving him until last night to surrender them. The Creekes are said to be willing to surrender the negroes, but it is thought they will not be able to do so, the negroes being too strong for them. It was difficult for the Chiefs Bushy Head and Addar to restrain the Cherokees from immediate vengeance, and they will be unable to keep them off the Creek territory longer than this morning.

There are 300 armed men now on the ground and more going. A fight is almost sure to take place to-day, as the negroes are about 200 strong and well armed. A large number left here last night for the battleground.

St. Louis, Aug. 4.—Private advises from Vinita, Indian Territory, referring to the recent disturbances between the Cherokee Indians and negroes belonging to the Creek Nation, say a compromise has just been of facted,—the Creek Indians agreeing to surrender the negroes who killed young Cobb and wounded young Cowan, two Cherokee boys, a few days ago.

CREEK VS. CHEROKEE. LITTLE Rock, Ark., Aug. 6.—Reports from Fort Smith of serious troubles at Muscogee, Creek Nation, between the Creek negroes and Cherokees, are received. Two Creek negro horse-thieves, Bill Peters and Long Monday, were hanged by the Cherokee lynchers on the 27th ult. On Wednesday thirteen Creek negroes crossed into the Cherokee Nation and shot two young Cherokees, William Cobb and Alec Cowan. The first was killed, and the latter fatally wounded. Dick Glass, a Creek, was killed also in the fight. At last accounts some 200 Cherokees were assembled at Fort Gibson, near the line, intending to attack the Creek negroes, also in force, only desisting at the interposition of Chiefs Bushyhend and Ross, who obtained a promise of suspension of hostilities if the thirteen Creek negroes were delivered to the Cherokees by Thursday morning last. A white man was reported killed on Tuesday last, which will require the interference of the Federal authorities. BROUGHT HIM DOWN. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. Springfield, Ill., Aug. 6.—This evening a negro named Billy Lewis was shot by L. W. Jamison, who resides on the fair-grounds. Jamison's family consists of his wife and a girl named Hattie Carpenter, aged 20. Mrs. Jamison came down-town after supper, and Jamison went out to call in Lewis, who soon put in an appearance in an intoxicated condition, and attempted to outrage the girl. He chased her back and forth through the house several times, and was in hot pursuit when Jamison returned. He followed the negro through the house, picked up a revolver, and ordered him to halt. Lewis did not obey, and Jamison fired three times, one ball entering Lewis' side between the ribs and hip, indicting a wound which may prove fatal. Jamison was arrested by some of his neighbors. There are several stories as to the circumstances of the shooting and those which led to it, but the facts appear to be about as stated. MAIL ROBBERY.
A special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LA Crosse, Wls.. Aug. 6. — Edward A. Keeler, who was arrested on Wednesday at Lanesboro for robbing a postal-car in this city of a number of registered letters Sunday, was arraigned before Justice Hubbard to-day and waived examination. He was bound over to the September term of the United States Court, ball being fixed at 50,000. Since Keeler has been confined in jail other strong proofs have been brought out to show him guilty, he having been at the business for over a year. How much he has taken cannot be uncertained. It is thought he cannot furnish ball. United States District-Attorney H. M. Lewis, of Madison, is here in the interest of the Government in the prosecution; also Chief Clerk Ed S. Bean, of the Mail Service, St. Paul, and J. D. King, Post-Office Inspector, Chicago. They will give the case a thorough investigation.

SENTENCED.

NEW YORK, Aug. 6.—In the General Session to-day, J. Lloyd Haigh, the well-known wire-rope manufacturer and contractor for the wire of the East River bridge, who by means of false acceptances caused the suspension of the Grocers' Bank, was arraigned for forgery in the third degree. Through counsel he pleaded guilty, stating that he had done all in his power to repair the injury committed, and implored a light sentence. Judge Gildersleeve severely reprimanded the prisoner, and sentenced him to hard labor in the State Prison for four years. The spiedful charge to which Haigh pleaded guilty was forgery of a draft dated Dec. 15, 1879, for $4,495.19, payable to and signed by himself, and accepted by Barney & Ferris, of Sandusky, O.

"SPIELMARK" SHOVERS.

INDIANAPOLIS, Inq., Aug. 6.—United States Commissioner Milligan, in the case of the United States vs. Harry Murdock and Joseph Leross, held to-day that spleimarks bore such a resemblance to genuine coin as to deceive a man of ordinary prudence under ordinary circumstances, and in default of $500 ball each of the defendants were committed to answer to the charge of uttering counterfeit coin. In size, color, and general appearance these spleimarks very much resemble $10 and $50 gold pieces, and defendants were using them as evidences of wealth to entrap an ignorant countryman into investing good money and receiving the spurious in return by means of a lottery scheme. The case is a novel one.

A CHINESE DESPERADO.

NEW YORK, Aug. 6—Qulimbo Appo, son of the notorious Chinese murderer, drank, gambled, and quarroled with a young man named John Collins last night. Appo is an expert at cards, and won all Collins' money. The latter said he was cheated, and the Chiuaman plunged a knife into his abdomen, ripping his victim open in a horrible manner. Collins is now on his deathbed. Appo is a noted desperado, and has served a number of terms in prison. His father cut open the heart of James Keoley in 1876. Fifteen years ago he assassinated his wife. He is at present under life sentence at Sing Sing.

A STABBING AFFRAY.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. RALKIGH, N. C., Aug. 6.—A probably fatal affray about a dog took place in Johnston County to-day between Darling Jones and John Black. Finally Black whipped out a

knife and stabbed Jones twice in the back, inflicting probably fatal wounds. His blood being well up by this time, Black, with his bloody knife, ran amuck through the crowd near by, slashing right and left, but doing no further fatal damage. He was overpowered and taken to jail.

DISCHARGED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
SPRINGFIELD, Ill., Aug. 6.—Charles Carter, of Rochester, Sangamon County, was arrested on the charge of obtaining goods on false pretenses from Ingraham, Corbin & May, Chicago. At the examination before Justice Schroyer, the prosecution showed that Carter had represented himself to be worth $10,000 on March 2, and had since admitted that his homestead, which he had put down in his statement to the firm at $3,000, was worth only $750. He was discharged on the ground that it was not shown that he was not worth $10,000 on March 2, as he then represented.

CALIFORNIA HANGING.
CALIFORNIA, Aug. 6.—John McGuire, who, while an inmate of the Penitentiary a year ago serving a sentence for murder, killed a fellow-convict, William E. Andrews, was hunged at San Rapael to-day.

A PREACHER MURDERED.

GALVESTON, Aug. 6.—The News' special from Ennis says: R. L. Edwards, a Christian preacher, was called out of his house and shot dead last night by unknown parties.

MILWAUKEE, Wis., Aug. 6.—All the gambling places in this city were ordered closed to-day, owing to the rapid increase in the business and the unusual prevalence of crime.

POST-OFFICE ROBBED.
DETROIT, Mich., Aug. 6.—The Post-Office at Erie, Mich., was entered last night, the safe blown up, and $1,375 stolen.

Dallas, Tex., Aug. 27.—This afternoon Allen Wright was hung for the murder of Jessie Wicks. Both were colored men. Nearly 3,000 people gathered round the scaffold, the women predominating. Some cowboys came
by 3,000 people gathered round the scaffold, the women predominating. Some cowboys came hundreds of miles to see the execution. The condemned man was to have been executed last Friday, but Gov. Roberts, in answer to a numerously-signed petition, granted him a respite till to-day, in order to better prepare for death.

PALESTINE, Tex., Aug. 27.—Great excitement has been caused here by the announcement that Roland Rucker, who was to have been hanged here to-day for the murder of R.P. Grayson and wife, had committed suicide. When the prison authorities visited his cell at 5 o'clock this morning they found the man in the last agonies of death. Near him was a large pool of blood, and blood was issuing from a wound in his left wrist, which he had made with a penknife. On examination it was found that the arteries had been severed. How Rucker got possession of the knife is a mystery.

KU-KLUXED THE WRONG NEGRO.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

CINCINNATI, O., Aug. 27.—A case of Ku-Kluxing with a happy termination occurred near Cochran, Ga., night before last. At midnight John Brown, a peaceable negro citizen, was aroused by the demands of two armed and disguised men for entrance. They declared they had come there to whip him. Brown replied that he was at home, but that he would not open the door, and would not be whipped. The men grew furious, fired at Brown twice, when he seized a shotgun and let them have two heavy loads of buckshot. Both fell dead, having received the charge in their heads. Brown recognized them as Frank and Mack Dykes, two young farmers with whom he recently had a difficulty about work. He notified the authorities, and a Coroner's Inquest was held over the bodies in the presence of a great crowd. The verdict declares that Brown acted only in self-defense, and a good portion of the public Indorse his course. Many citizens approve his pluck and promise him any assistance he may need.

THE ATTACK UPON GEORGIA NEGROES.
GOVERNOR COLQUITT HAS SEVEN WHITE MEN ARRESTED—FEARS OF A RESCUE.

ATLANTA, July 31.—Governor Colquitt went to Jonesboro' last night with the Gate City Guard, of Atlanta, to prevent any attempt on the part of friends to rescue the prisoners who were put in jail there on a charge of the murder of Millie Johnson, colored, and of fatally beating her father and mother, and fatally wounding her brother.

Jonesboro' was in a great state of excitement over the affair all yesterday. Sheriff Archer met with resistance in attempting to arrest some persons charged with the crime. Seven prisoners were brought to Atlanta by the Gate City Guard and put in jail here for safekeeping. Others will probably be arrested. Samuel Cook, one of the prisoners, turned State's evidence and implicated all of the others, but subsequently retracted and said he was frightened into confession. There is an uncompromising demand for a full investigation, and if the guilty parties are found Georgia will have a wholesale hanging.

KU KLUX AMUSEMENT.
WORSE THAN WEAVER REPORTED TO AN INTELLIGENCER REPORTER.
The Terrible Crime Perpetrated at Jonesboro, Ga.—The Citizens of Atlanta Aroused Over the Outrage— How Negroes are Killed for Sport.
miles of Atlanta there occurred last night one of the most flagrant outrages recorded in the history crime. The victims were unoffending negroes, and the perpetrators fifteen white roughs, disguised by fiendish streaks of black across their faces, and looking in the glare of the torches they carried like veritable demons. The circumstances of the outrage are almost too horrible to tell, and the surroundings sickened your correspondent as he saw them. An aged negro and his wife, with their garments dyed in their own blood, which a brutal beating had made to gush from their flesh; a young negress lying dead between her two crying children, with a bullet in her brain, and a lad of sixteen groaning in the agony of an awful pistol wound in his side. Such a scene I beheld in a poor log cabin, while around it crowded a hundred negroes, trying to aid and comfort their afflicted friends, and a few kind hearted white friends furnishing what they needed. The history of this crime is as follows:

One year ago Joe Thompson, a negro fifty years old, was at work on the farm of James McElroy, in Fayette county. John Gray, McElroy's brother-in-law, came one day into the field where Joe and his son Bob were at work. He accused Bob of stealing a plow from him. Bob denied that he had done so. Gray grew angry and struck the boy. His father interfered to prevent him from being beaten. Gray then turned and severely beat the old man, who could offer but a feeble resistance. Joe left the place at once, taking his family with him and obtained employment with Reuben Munday, in Clayton county, where he now lives. He prosecuted Gray for assault and battery. The Superior Court fined the young bulldozer $100 and costs, thus greatly outraging him and his friends. Joe feared their vengeance, but he had a good friend in Mr. Munday, and all went well with him until night before last. He was asleep in his cabin with his wife by his side. In the same room were his married daughter, Millie Johnson, with her two small children, and Bob Thompson, the boy whom Gray had struck in the field. About midnight Joe was aroused by the noise of voices in the yard. Peering through a crack in the door he saw fifteen men with half a dozen huge torches. Nearly all of them were armed, and on the face of each were broad streaks and splotches of soot to serve as a disguise.

The old negro knew that he was to be the victim of this mob, for almost as soon as he had seen them they rushed upon the door and began to knock it in. Some of them seized a log in the side of the cabin and tore it from its place. Soon the door was down and the villains were in and ready for their bloody work. Two of them seized Joe Thompson and dragged him out. They held him down while a third beat him with a stick until the blood literally spotted from his body. He was left almost dead with deep gashes across his back and breast and his bald head horribly cut. I saw him next morning and the blood was scarcely dry on the rough shirt it had dyed with its deep crimson.

His old wife had suffered with him. She was beaten by a ruffian until she fell senseless to the earth. As the mob continued this infamous work, young Bob arose from his bed and made a movement to help his old parents. He was floored by a shot which pierced his side near the lungs. Millie Johnson lay in the bed terrified almost to death. She attempted to rise and was shot in the head to fall back a corpse. Her little children on either side clung in terror to their dead mother for protection.

After completing this outrage the band moved off, and continued its villiany by firing into the house of Clarke Goddard, a peaceable negro living two miles further down the road. Soon after this they met two white men and threatened their lives.

The news of the night's horror was heralded over the county by sunrise, and created among all good people the greatest excitement. The sheriff, with a posse, scoured the district, and before noon arrested John Gray, Lewis Gray, Sam Cook and James McElroy. Subsequently six other men were arrested and carried to Jonesboro, where they were jailed. Negroes and whites flocked to town to discuss the outrage, and to consider what was best to be done. All day yesterday Jonesboro was in a state of excitement. Nobody offered any palliation for the awful crime, and on all hands there were demands for strict justice. All the circumstances seem to point to the guilt of Grav and his friends. Joe Thompson says that a few days ago McElroy came to his house, ostensibly to get him to make a tray; but while there acted in such a way as to arouse grave suspicions in the negro's mind.

About dark last night there was circulated in Jonesboro a rumor that the friends of the prisoners in Fayette county had organized a strong armed band, and intended to raid Jonesboro and rescue the accused. The Sheriff summoned a posse to guard the jail, but as they were poorly armed he telegraphed Gov. Colquitt the state of affairs, and asked that a company be sent out at once to protect the town. The Governor ordered out the Gate City Guard, which left with eighty men on a special train. The military found the town in great excitement. They at once surrounded the jail, and assured the people that the public peace should be protected. The Guard were accompanied by the Governor himself, who did much to allay the turbulence. The troops have just returned to Atlanta, bringing the prisoners with them to be safely jailed here. Atlanta is fully aroused over this outrage. Several leading attorneys have been engaged to prosecute the case. Gov. Colquitt will offer a reward of $500 for any other parties implicated in the affair. The people Georgia are determined that such an outrage shall be punished as the law directs, and as humanity demands.
joe-thompson-jonesboro-1880-07-29.A8:
"Not A Happy One."

BY C. J. STODDARD.

A Demoniac and Dastardly Deed in Georgia.

The Atlanta Constitution publishes the following: "About 12 o'clock Wednesday night a party of ten or fifteen disguised men went to the house of Joe Thompson, a quiet old negro who works on the farm of Mr. Reuben Munday, two and a half miles beyond Jonesboro. As they approached the little log house in which the negro and his family were sleeping, they began the most demoniac yells and screams. Rushing upon the door, they began to force an entrance. They carried torches of rags saturated with kerosene. The light dazzled the negro, and the fierce assault on the door terrified him so that he did not know what to do. He had no weapon in his house but an old pistol, and he could not find this. He rushed to the door and pressed as hard as he could, but the howling mob dashed it in and pushed him on the floor. While part of the assailants pressed the door, others tore a log out of the house and made a big opening, through which they fired. As soon as the mob got into the room, in which a whole family of terrified negroes were huddled in horror, wild with rage the yelling men seized old Thompson and dragged him out into the yard. Here two men held him to the ground while a third beat him with a stick, drawing blood at every blow and splitting the scalp of his bald head in several places. His breast was gashed and the blood literally spouted from his body. While part of the men were doing this others seized the old woman and beat her as furiously as their fellows were belaboring her husband. Her screams were unavailing and she was left almost dead. But this was not the worst. Millie Johnson, a married daughter of Joe Thompson, was lying in bed with two little children by her side. She raised up to see what was the cause of the alarm and just then was shot in the brain and fell back dead. Young Bob Thompson, a boy of sixteen, tried to help his parents, but was shot down by a bullet in his side which will probably be fatal. After doing this work so completely, the crowd left the scene, leaving one negro dead and three bleeding."

The people of Jonesboro, both white and colored, were greatly incensed at the outrage. Steps were at once taken to arrest the perpetrators. The next day seven white men were arrested, one of whom was identified and another confessed. The friends of the arrested men threatened to rescue them from the officers and Governor Colquitt ordered a company of Atlanta militia to Jonesboro. He also went there himself to calm the excitement. The press and people of Georgia call for the severe punishment of the ruffians, but it is doubtful if any conviction can be obtained.

ATLANTA, Ga., July 31.—To the Editor of the Cincinnati Commercial: One of the most horrible outrages ever committed upon negroes by the Southern whites has just been perpetrated near Jonesboro, twenty miles from Atlanta. No crime of the Ku-Klux era ever surpassed it in malignity and atrocious brutality. And when we look back upon the quondam methods of the Southern Democracy for establishing their supremacy, we may justly call this the opening of the Presidential campaign in the South. To the negro race this outrage seems the return of the age of terror. The hand of oppression that took from them the rights that were given by the shedding of blood they feel laid upon them again. They anticipate now the return of the methods and of the spirit of Ku-Kluxism. The whole affair is not only a disgrace to the State of Georgia, but a travesty upon the civilization of the nineteenth century and the boasted freedom of our Republic.

About a year ago Joe Thompson, an aged and decrepit negro, was, with his family, employed in Fayette County, Georgia, on the cotton plantation of John Gray. Thompson's son, a negro of 10 years, was accused by his employer of the theft of a plow, and Gray, disregarding the ordinary and slow forms of justice, one day administered a horrible whipping to him in the fields. Thompson had Gray arrested on a charge of assault and battery, and so strong was the testimony against him and so conclusive the evidence that the young negro was innocent of the theft, that Gray was found guilty, even before a Georgia jury, and a fine of $100 was imposed upon this castigator. Gray now threatened Thompson and his family with death, and the poor negro was, with his family, forced to leave his unharvested crop and flee to an adjoining county. He settled on a plantation two miles from Jonesboro, in Claythe county, and up to night before last lived there unmolested, winning for himself in the community a reputation for honesty and industry. In the above facts, an outrage in themselves, is found the only cause for a second outrage, one of the most horrible of all those that have occurred in the South since the emancipation.

In a rude log cabin, about twelve feet square, night before last, Joe Thompson and his family—a wife, son, married daughter and her two children—huddled themselves together for a night's rest. Little did they dream that their troubles of a year ago were to return to them that night in a horrible and hideous form. About midnight the inmates of the rude cabin were startled from their sleep by the crushing in of the door and the tearing of a log from the side of their humble home. They opened their eyes upon a scene that would terrify the most dauntless hearts.—a scene not strange to those negroes of the South who have lived through the era of Ku Kluxism. A score of armed men, with painted faces, hideous in disguise, bearing torches made of rags saturated with kerosene, yelling like demons, thronged into the door. Four seized the aged father by arms and legs, threatening, "G—d—n you, we came here to give you a good thrashing," and bore him toward the door; four others seized the son. The daughter, sleeping between her two children, raised up in bed, but a bullet went crashing through her skull and she fell back a corpse, her warm blood spurting out in the faces of her innocent children. Meanwhile the father, ignorant of his daughter's death, had been borne out of doors into the field. Four men swung him from the ground by arms and legs, while a fifth administered the lash upon his face and body, incarring him terribly. Near by four others of the flends held his son, while a similar barbarous torture was inflicted upon him, until finally, in his thirst for blood, one of the midnight assassins put a bullet through the young negro's body from side to side. Their hearts were still insatiate for blood. They reentered the house, dragged Joo Thompson's aged and unoffending wife from her bed, and inflicted upon her a whipping no less brutal than that which they had just inflicted upon father and son. Yelling and waving their torches aloft, the assassins then departed, marking the path of their return by firing into a neighboring negro's house on their way. Joo Thompson soon recovered consciousness, and, dragging his bleeding limbs about his home, found his son lying fatally wounded in the field, his daughter lying dead between her children, and his wife mourning pitifully and bleeding from the effects of the lash.

Joo Thompson had recognized among the murderers John Gray, the former oppressor, and James McElroy, a brother-in-law of this human flend. On the following morning these two men were arrested for murder and incarcerated in the Jonesboro Jail.

It seems a terrible thing that even fifteen men could have been found in one county in Georgia who would hand together and deliberately march fifteen miles to the commission of such a crime as this. But subsequent events proved that a large class of the residents of that county sympathized with them in this outrage, and traveled in arms to Jonesboro to effect their release from jail. Late last night Gov. Colquitt received a telegram from the Sheriff of Jonesboro asking him to order the military to that place immediately. Ten men had been arrested, suspected of complicity in the outrage, and a large crowd had arrived in the city from Fayette County, and demanded the release of the prisoners. The jail was then guarded by fifty armed men, but a collusion was momentarily expected. Gov. Colquitt, escorted by the Gate City Guards, repaired to the scene at midnight last night, quelled the riot, and returned to Atlanta with the ten prisoners to-day. The negroes of the community, outraged as they have been, have raised no hand against their oppressors, nor even held an indignation meeting. Submissive as brutes, they bow hopelessly beneath the brutality that has been practiced upon their race. The whites of Jonesboro have held an indignation meeting, offered a reward for the apprehension of the murderers, and ain't great consternation from the fear that this outrage will be used to the detriment of the Democratic party in the present campaign.

It is true that this affair is of momentous political significance. It illustrates the methods of the Southern Democracy. It points out the slight esteem in which the life of a negro, to say nothing of his rights, is held in the South. It tells in unmistakable language that for reasons far less trivial than any political ones, negroes are slaughtered in the South without mercy and without cause. No more cold-blooded, objectless murder than this which I have recorded can be found in the annals of crime. But it has a higher significance than a political one; it cries aloud for a change of moral principles, as well as political ones. It demands the abolishment of a negro slavery far worse than that one that was characterized by barter and trade of human souls. It cries out for redress to every honest lover of justice and humanity. And unless there soon comes a change in both the moral and political tone of the South, the negro will be driven from the land of his birth, or ingulfed in a slavery tenfold more terrible than any he has ever known.

The late outrage at Jonesboro, Georgia, is creating quite a sensation.
The late outrage at Jonesboro, Georgia, is creating quite a sensation and excitement everywhere throughout that State. It appears that a band of some twenty masked men repaired to the residence of one Joe Thompson (colored) on the night of the 28th ult., and beat him very severely, as also his wife, and murdered his daughter. Some of the maskers were recognized by Thompson, who avers that they belong to the higher classes of the community of Jonesboro. The difficulty originated in the fact that Thompson had testified against one of these worthies on a trial before one of the justice's courts, and that his testimony was very damaging in its effect. No other cause is assigned for the outrage committed upon this peaceable family than that. The accused parties have all been arrested and jailed. The threats of the negroes are so alarming, and the excitement so great, that Governor Colquitt has ordered the militia of the county to go down from Atlanta, as it is feared the negroes will try to lynch the prisoners.

Vicksburg Herald.

In Jonesboro, Georgia, recently a colored woman and her brother were killed by a gang of roughs because the father of the negroes had one of the roughs indicted for assault and battery. In Richmond, Ohio, recently a colored woman returning from a colored camp meeting was shot in the stomach and killed by white desperadoes. In isolated cases, North and South, the weaker race is often imposed on. In any part of the world where two races live together the weaker race is always more or less mistreated. In fact, individuals of the same race are constantly maltreating each other. It is human nature to err.

We merely refer to these facts to remind those people in the North who are howling so much about the Jonesboro affair, that they have no room to howl because it was committed on Southern soil. Such affairs occur just as frequently, and perhaps more frequently in proportion to the number of colored people on Northern soil. The Richmond, Ohio, affair was fully as brutal, fatal and deplorable as that at Jonesboro, Georgia. Both were grievous wrongs, and good people everywhere regret them, and are striving and will continue to strive to punish and prevent them. Public sentiment North is not one whit more opposed to such things than public sentiment South. The Georgia affair was bitterly denounced by every newspaper of standing in the State and by the leading papers outside of the State. Gov. Colquitt called out the State forces to arrest the guilty parties and the outraged law will doubtless be promptly vindicated. Can as much be said of the outrage at Richmond, Ohio?

The story of the outrage on the Thompson family, colored, by night-riders in Georgia, shows how the barbarism that inspired kukluxism survives. Nowhere, except in one of the ex-slave States, is such an atrocity possible. It is such as nowhere, even in the South, would the worst outlaws dare attempt to perpetrate upon anybody except negroes. To the night-riders who disgrace the South, disgrace our civilization, and disgrace humanity, the "d-d nigger" seems created to be hunted down and horsewhipped and shot in cold blood as the members of this colored family were. And while the Governor of Georgia, to his credit, has maintained the law against mob violence in the case, it is none the less significant of the barbarous sentiment pervading the State, that the military had to be called out to prevent the rescue by a mob of the perpetrators of the atrocity.—Inter Ocean.

The Impressions of a Buckeye Rambler in Dixie.
Politics, Politicians, Incidents, Etc.
No. IV.
BY W. S. S.
Doubtless long ere this the news of that infamous outrage committed upon a colored family in Clayton county, Georgia, has reached the ears of many of your readers. Words are inadequate to express one's indignation; the English vocabulary is too scant; the deed was diabolical in the extreme. It threw the community into utter confusion. The relentless hands of the murderers drew forth the sympathy of the entire State in behalf of the victims. The facts seem to be these: Some time ago a young white man and a colored man had a little trouble relative to a plow. The white fellow beat the colored man severely. The father of the colored man indicted the white fellow for assault and battery. He secured a verdict, notwithstanding the opposition. This sottled the matter for a while. Some weeks ago a band of ruffians, disguised, at a late hour, attacked the house of this old gentleman (Mr. Thompson), who had figured in the trial just mentioned, and demanded admittance. He, suspecting, of course, refused to comply. Several demands were made, with threats; but with a similar result. Finally they attempted to break open the door. The old colored gentleman and his son were resisting the devils from within. At the same time one of their number (the fiends), went to the corner of the house and peeled off a board, making quite an opening, as the house was a log one. In this room was the old colored man's daughter, Millie Johnson, asleep with her two children on either side of her. She, hearing the noise, raised up in bed. At this juncture one of the ruffians fired through the opening he had made, shot the young woman through the breast, producing a fatal wound, and she falling back, weltering in her own blood, died between her two children. The old gentleman (Mr. Thompson), was severely beaten; also his wife; and their son was mortally wounded. How sad! What a crime! Will the culprits be punished? Will they be hung? That is a problem. You can't find a jury in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred that will convict a white man for murdering a Negro. To deceive the Republicans of the North they will cry out, "Hang them! hang them! hang them! Let not one of them escape!" This is all a hoax. These rebels do not mean to punish a white man for the simple offense of killing two or three Negroes. Judging from the papers, the inhabitants of the immediate vicinity are anxious that justice be meted out to them. Governor Colquitt, with the Gate City Guards, was sent for to prevent the friends of the prisoners from taking them out of jail. One fellow, who had turned State's evidence, afterward denied what he had said, declaring that he was frightened into it and had told what was not true for the truth. We shall wait and see what the result will be. If these three "K's," as they are sometimes called, are acquitted, the colored people ought by all means to lynch every one of them. I have given you a sketch of the crime, and only a sketch. We will not dwell in this region longer.

I spoke of the gubernatorial convention in one of my communications. I told you how the Democracy was divided from the center to the circumference. I also stated that there was a possibility of their failing to make a nomination. Well, my predictions were true. They could not agree, and after thirty-three ballots the ex-Confederates gave it up in despair, and decided to nominate all the State officers except the Governor, leaving this part of the role until they had tried their hand upon other victims. This they did, and on the eighth day of the convention they tried again to nominate a Governor, but did not succeed. Every clique stuck to its favorite. Alexander H. Stephens tried to pour a little healing balm over their sore heads, but this, like spirits of turpentine, only made it smart. The two-thirds rule was the trouble the convention could not climb over. They finally adjourned, recommending that the people vote for Governor Colquitt in the October election. The minority, after the majority had left for their several homes, called a special convention to make known their grievances, and to ask the sympathy of the people on the ground that they had been outraged and trampled on by the majority of their Democratic brethren. In conclusion I would point to the fact that these very men who are seeking to control the Nation can not manage their own affairs at home.

ONCE GREENBACKER, NOW REPUBLICAN.

TALK WITH S. R. MASON, WHO WAS THE GREENBACK CANDIDATE FOR GOVERNOR OF PENNSYLVANIA IN 1878—WHY HE CHANGED HIS PARTY RELATIONS.

S. R. Mason, of Mercer, Penn., who in 1878 was the Greenback candidate for Governor of Pennsylvania, receiving nearly 100,000 votes, has recently joined the Republican party. A short time ago he was staying at the Fifth Avenue Hotel, and a TRIBUNE reporter had a conversation with him.

"What is your opinion in regard to the Republi-
“What is your opinion in regard to the Republican party in Western Pennsylvania, and what progress is being made?” was asked.

“I have not been long enough in the Republican counsels to give you exact figures, but Western Pennsylvania has always been solid for the Republican party, and it will be so this fall. There is no disaffection in the party there at all. All the misunderstandings of the past have been made up; the party organization is perfect, and the campaign will be an earnest and lively one.”

“How about the Greenback party there?”

“The party still has its organization, and has put its local ticket in the field, but its strength has waned greatly. In our county I do not think its whole vote can exceed 300.”

“You of course believed in the Greenback theories until resumption was an accomplished fact?”

“Resumption having been accomplished, the issues on which the National party fought were substantially settled, and that party naturally began going into a decline. I felt that I no longer had any business in it then, and must join another party. The Democratic party was dealing altogether with dead issues, and I could not be happy there. I had had enough of a mortuary aspect of things in the Greenback party, and I wanted to get among the living again. Seriously, however, I believe in the principles and policy of the Republican party. I believe they are the wisest and best suited to the varied interests of the whole people of the country, and that is the reason I have come into its ranks.”

“Will many of the Greenbackers in your neighborhood follow your example?”

“They will; and while my belief is that the Greenbackers, as a general thing, will settle back into their old parties, that very fact will result in large accessions to the Republican ranks. The National party was made up from the two parties, each of which appeared to contribute in proportion to its size, and of course in the North the Republican element was much the greater. I think that at least three-fourths of that party will support one or the other of the old parties. Thus of course will help the Republicans. However, many who were Democrats before may come ever to the Republican
least three months of that party will support one of the other of the old parties. This of course will help the Republicans. However, many who were Democrats before may come over to the Republican party, just as many Democrats themselves are doing."

"What effect do you think Weaver's candidacy will have?"

"Weaver's candidacy will merely have the effect of withholding about one-quarter of the old Greenback party from voting with the other two parties. Weaver cannot carry a single State, and I do not think he will have such a following from either party, in any State, as to change the result. In Maine, where the Democrats and Greenbackers have united, the Republicans will carry the State over both. In Pennsylvania the Fusionists will have a stronger showing. Two Creek negro horse-thieves, Bill Peters and Long Monday, were hanged by the Cherokee lynchers on the 27th ult. Lloyd Haigh, the well-known wire-rope manufacturer and contractor for the wire of the East River bridge, who by means of false acceptances caused the suspension of the Grocers' Bank, was arraigned for forgery in the third degree. "SPIELMARK" SHOVERS.

INDIANAPOLIS, Inq., Aug. 6.—United States Commissioner Milligan, in the case of the United States vs. Harry Murdock and Joseph Leross, held to-day that spleimarks bore such a resemblance to genuine coin as to deceive a man of ordinary prudence under ordinary circumstances, and in default of $500 ball each of the defendants were committed to answer to the charge of uttering counterfeit coin. In size, color, and general appearance these spleimarks very much resemble $10 and $50 gold pieces, and defendants were using them as evidences of wealth to entrap an ignorant countryman into investing good money and receiving the spurious in return by means of a lottery scheme. The case is a novel one.

A CHINESE DESPERADO.

NEW YORK, Aug. 6—Qulimbo Appo, son of the notorious Chinese murderer, drank, gambled, and quarroled with a young man named John Collins last night. Appo is an expert at cards, and won all Collins' money. The latter said he was cheated, and the Chiuaman plunged a knife into his abdomen, ripping his victim open in a horrible manner. Collins is now on his deathbed. Appo is a noted desperado, and has served a number of terms in prison. His father cut open the heart of James Keoley in 1876. Fifteen years ago he assassinated his wife. He is at present under life sentence at Sing Sing.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill., Aug. 7.—William Lewis, the colored man who was shot at the fairgrounds last night, as noted in these dispatches, died to-night about 6 o'clock. At the Coroner's inquest it was developed that there was a criminal intimacy between L. W. Jamison, the man who done the shooting, and Hattie Carpenter, the girl who lived in the family, and whose attempted rape was the pretense for the shooting. Lewis made a dying statement to the effect that he caught Jamison and the girl in improper relations, and that she first attempted to shoot him, but failed, and Jamison took the revolver and shot him. A QUEER PROSECUTION. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribute.
St. Louis, Aug. 7. A patient died at the City Hospital to-day under circumstances that will give rise to a peculiar prosecution. His name was Wesley Washington, and he was a professional burglar. A week ago he broke into the brussels-foundry of O. P. Chamberlain & Co., No. 13 Spruce strook, intending to rob the place. It seems that there had been several burglaries committed there, and the proprietors had rigged up an old musket with a wire attached to the trigger and stretched across the main room. The gun was pointed so that it was bound to hit whatever pulled the wire. Washington got into the place, and in the darkness walked against the wire, the charge taking effect in his leg. He had strength enough to scramble out into the alley, but was caught therby the police. The leg was amputated, but, as the man was scorfulous, blood-polishing resulted, and death occurred to-day. There is a statute in this State making it a criminal offense to set such a trap for a human being. The prisoner confessed before death that he went on the promises to commit a burglary. Novorothless, the case will be investigated tomorrow by the Coroner as a criminal case involving the proprietor of the foundry.

HELD FOR MURDER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
SPRINGFIELD, Ill., Aug. 8.—The Coroner's inquest upon the negro Billy Lewis, who was shot by L. W. Jamison Friday night, was continued to-day. The testimony presented showed even more conclusively than that of yesterday that it was a case of deliberate murder. It was shown that Jamison habitually carried a pistol, and that he had threatened several of his neighbors. The testimony made it clear that the negro was murdered for fear he would make public the criminal relations between Jamison and the girl Hattle Carpenter, who made herself notorious two years ago by publicly cowhiding a tailor who had made disparging remarks about her. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

TORONTO, Aug. 8.—At a meeting held here of the delegates from the municipalities through which the Toronto, Grey & Bruce Railway passes, a scheme for expending $900,000 towards altering the gauge of the road and then lensing it to the Grand Trunk for a period of twenty-one years, was submitted and unanimously endorsed by those present.

It is proposed to establish a cotton-factory here on the cooperative principle; the factory to be run by steam, and the capital to be $200,000.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

MONTREAL, Aug. 8.—The shipment of cheese from the port of Montreal last week reached over 28,000 boxes. Of butter 8,140 packages were shipped.

The board of Agriculture has decided to send a delegate to the New York Dairymen's Fair, to acquaint himself with the requisits for the working dairy exhibit in the show at Montreal in 1881.

The Health Office has prepared a statement showing that the death-rate per 1,000 in Montreal of those over 5 years of age is 12, against 14.01 in New York, 12.70 in Boston, and 13.22 in London, Eng. The death-rate per 1,000 under 5 years of age is 18.61 in Montreal, 10.17 in London, 8 in Boston, and 11.91 in New York. The birth-rate in Montreal is 47 per 1,000, while in London, Eng., it is only 30. The greater number of the infants who are entered in the bills of mortality do not belong to the city, but are foundlings brought from all parts of Canada and the United States to the Grey Nunnery, where they are abandoned by their parents.

The number of sea-going vessels which have arrived up to the present time is 331, against 270 for the corresponding period last year.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

St. JOHN, N. B., Aug. 8.—Sailors are unusually source at St. John just now, and the few on hand are demanding very high rates. A number of sailors who shipped the other day received $60 for the run across the Atlantic,—the old rate having been $25 and $30.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Quebec, Aug. 8.—A large number of cases of house-breaking are reported since the use of street-lamps has been discontinued. In one night six different houses were broken into in Montreal Ward. Numerous petty accidents—such as colliding with lamp-posts and telegraph-poles, and narrow escapes from being run over—are being reported.

In no one branch is the civic service properly furnished. Neither the police nor the fire service is maintained as it ought to be. The city is in total darkness at night, and the result promises to be well nigh disastrous to the credit of Quebec.

The number of son-going vessels entered inwards at the Quebec Custom-House from the opening of navigation up to yesterday is 453; the clearances to the same time, including steamers at out-ports, are 485,—leaving sixty-eight vessels in port and in the small out-ports. There are also thirty-five vessels in the Port of Montreal. Since the opening of navigation 110 vessels have been licensed by the Quebec Custom-House for the local trade of the Province; 1,200 market steamers and schooners have arrived in port since the opening of navigation.

At the Sligo iron mills in Allegheny county, Michael Fenton leaned against a pile of iron plates. They fell over on him and crushed him to death.

While engaged in tearing down a derrick at Beaver City, the crown block fell and struck a man named Croy on the head, badly cutting it open across the top.

Catherine Grant, New Brunswick, N. J., was so badly burned while attempting to light a fire with kerosene, on Friday, that she died the next morning.

L. W. Jamison, a horse-trainer, at Springfield, Ill., shot and fatally wounded William Lewis, a negro, on Friday night, for attempting to feloniously assault Hattie White, a young servant girl.

A switch-tender, named Emery, who resided at South Easton, was run over and instantly killed on Saturday afternoon by a train, a short distance above the Lehigh and Susquehana railroad depot.

M. H. Kimball, a hardware merchant on Broadway, Baltimore, was drowned while bathing at Bay Ridge. He was not missed until the bathing suit which he had hired was sought.

In a Meadville hardware store Willie Hanratty, aged 15, was passing under a hoisting apparatus, where a heavy stove was being raised when the rope broke and the boy was crushed beneath it, cutting a fearful gash in his head, breaking both his legs and internally injuring him.

The body of Patrick Corcoran, aged 24, was found on the third pier of the Tenth street bridge, Pittsburgh, with his skull fractured and several other wounds on his head, evidently made with some blunt instrument. It is supposed he was murdered in some house near by and carried to this point.

The bark Nova Scotia, Captain Kibbell, loaded with 3,300 barrels of naphtha and lying at Williamsburg, was burned last night. Loss, $45,000. The flames extended to the barks Antonette and Cyclone, also loaded with naphtha, and caused damage of $10,000 to each.
Mr. Walter Bryan, Sr., a Philadelphia millionare, aged 77, who was temporarily staying at the Hyde House, Ridgeway, Elk county, rose from his bed while asleep and jumped from the window a considerable distance to the ground, receiving injuries which resulted in his death the following day.

At Franklin Square, near Hempstead, L. L., on the farm of Charles Hickman, a row occurred between two of his farm hands, Gautieg Yajan and George Govlin, in which the former cut Govlin's hand with a siekle, inflicting a dangerous wound. Yajan was pursued and captured by the citizens. Govlin may die.

Burt Keith, a farmer of Girard township, Erie county, becoming enraged at one of his horses for some reason or other, took it by the tongue with his hands and tore the member loose at the roots. The cruel farmer was arrested and taken before a justice of the peace where he plead guilty to avoid exposing the evidence, and was fined $10 and costs—$4.39.

John Sharer was digging a cellar, and during the day his little daughter brought him a lunch of bread and coffee. While he was eating, the bank above him began to give way, and the girl cried to her father to take care. Sharer, however, was so intent on getting his daughter out of danger that he was overtaken by the falling mass and died before assistance came.

Alexander Holland, treasurer of the American express company, who has a summer residence at West Park, on the Hudson, was terribly injured by his horses running away while out riding with his family. Mr. Holland was dragged over the dashboard at the heels of the horses, and badly bruised about the head and different parts of the body.

Thomas E. Shelbaker, keeper of an opera house on Vine street, Cincinnati, shot Policeman A. Clumley twice, once in the groin and once in the abdoman. Clumley will not survive. Snelbaker was under arrest at the time for a row in which he, Clumley's son, two of Clumley's daughters and Virgie Jackson, an actress, were engaged in a Vine street car.

The excursion propeller E. Corning, belonging to John H. Starin, was leaving Glen Island, with between 700 and 800 passengers, and while backing out from the pier, she ran her stern on a rock, stoving a hole in it, when she filled and sank to the guards. The passengers were transferred to the steamers Laura M. Starin and St. Nicholas, without any loss of life.

An old lady by the name of Pendergrast, who resided with her son on West Carson street, South Side, Pittsburgh, had gone up the road to gather coal and was not seen by the engineer until too close upon her to reverse the engine. He sounded the alarm, but the woman, who was between seventy-five and eighty years of age, no doubt failed to hear the whistle on account of the noise from the mill. Her head was entirely severed from her body, her bowels cut open and strewed along the track and otherwise horribly mutilated.

A WOULD-BE OUTRAGER SHOT
CHICAGO, August 7.—A Springfield dispatch says great excitement was caused there last night by the shooting at the fair grounds of a negro named Wm. Lewis by L. J. Jamison, a horse trainer. While Jamison was attending to the horses some distance from his house he heard an outcry from his young servant girl, Hattie White. Running to the house he found Lewis assaulting and trying to overpower her. He snatched up a pistol from the washstand, and as Lewis fled began shooting at him. The third shot struck Lewis in his right side, inflicting probably a fatal wound.—Jamison surrendered himself.
